title: Ἄνθρωπος καταθραύσας ἄγαλμα
titleEn: The Man Who Smashed the Statue
part: The Man Who Smashed the Statue (Chambry 61 · Perry 285)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 61 (= Perry 285). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἄνθρωπός τις ξύλινον θεὸν ἔχων πένης ὢν καθικέτευε τοῦ ἀγαθοποιῆσαι.
sentences.tr: Anthrōpos tis xylinon theon echōn penēs ōn kathiketeue tou agathopoiēsai.
sentences.l: A certain man, having a wooden god and being poor, kept entreating it to do him good.
sentences.n: The wooden θεός is a household image kept at home. τοῦ ἀγαθοποιῆσαι is an articular infinitive in the genitive after the verb of entreating — the article turns the infinitive into a noun, 'for the doing-good'. ἀγαθοποιέω is a late word, not classical Attic.

sentences.t: Ὡς οὖν ταῦτ’ ἔπραττε καὶ μᾶλλον ἐν πενίᾳ διῆγε, θυμωθείς, ἐκ τοῦ σκέλους ἄρας αὐτὸν τῷ τοίχῳ προσέκρουσε.
sentences.tr: Hōs oun taut’ epratte kai mallon en peniāi diēge, thymōtheis, ek tou skelous aras auton tōi toichōi prosekrouse.
sentences.l: So when he kept doing this and yet went on living the more in poverty, having grown angry, having lifted it by the leg he dashed it against the wall.
sentences.i: So when he kept doing this and only lived on the deeper in poverty, he grew angry, took the god by the leg and dashed it against the wall.
sentences.n: Ὡς with the imperfect for 'as long as, while' — the praying and the deepening poverty run on together. ἐκ τοῦ σκέλους, 'by the leg', ἐκ of what a thing hangs from when it is picked up.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ παραχρῆμα κλασθείσης, ἔρρευσε χρυσὸς ἐξ αὐτῆς, ὃν συναγαγὼν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐβόα· « Στρεβλὸς τυγχάνεις, ὡς οἶμαι, καὶ ἀγνώμων· τιμῶντά σε γὰρ οὐδὲν ὠφέλησάς με· τυπτήσαντα δὲ πολλοῖς καλοῖς ἠμείψω. »
sentences.tr: Tēs de kephalēs autou parachrēma klastheisēs, erreuse chrysos ex autēs, hon synagagōn ho anthrōpos eboa· « Streblos tynchaneis, hōs oimai, kai agnōmōn· timōnta se gar ouden ōphelēsas me· typtēsanta de pollois kalois ēmeipsō. »
sentences.l: And its head having been broken at once, gold flowed out of it, and the man, having gathered it up, cried out: « You are crooked, as I think, and unfeeling; for me honouring you, you benefited in nothing; but me striking you, you repaid with many good things. »
sentences.i: Its head broke at once and gold poured out of it; and the man gathered it up and cried: « Crooked you are, I think, and thankless: when I honoured you, you did me no good at all, but when I struck you, you paid me back with a heap of blessings. »
sentences.n: τιμῶντα and τυπτήσαντα are participles agreeing with με, 'me while honouring you', 'me once I had struck you' — the two moments set against each other, present against aorist. τυγχάνεις with an adjective and no participle stands simply for 'you are, as it turns out'. ἠμείψω is second person aorist middle of ἀμείβω, to repay.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐδὲν ὠφελήσεις σαυτὸν πονηρὸν ἄνδρα τιμῶν, αὐτὸν δὲ τύπτων πλέον ὠφεληθήσῃ.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ouden ōphelēseis sauton ponēron andra timōn, auton de typtōn pleon ōphelēthēsēi.
sentences.l: The fable shows that you will benefit yourself in nothing by honouring a wicked man, but by striking him you will be benefited more.
sentences.n: The participles τιμῶν and τύπτων carry the condition, 'if you honour… if you strike…'. οὐδέν is an accusative of extent, 'in no respect'; ὠφεληθήσῃ is future passive, 'you will be benefited'.
